bibl.title: Word and picture identification: Is representational parsimony possible?

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: The most important result from the series of experi ments reported here is that repetition priming is observed when a test word is preceded by a line drawing of the same concept.

span.label: repetition priming between pictures and printed words
span.quote: In summary, Experiment 1 was designed to determine the presence and the extent of transfer between pictures and words under repetition priming conditions.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Four experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposition that although prior exposure to a printed word facilitates identification of a corresponding picture, exposure to a picture does not facilitate subsequent word recognition (Durso & Johnson, 1979).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repetition priming arises because processing an item changes the system, and the change facilitates later identification in proportion to how many of the same processes are re-invoked at test.
span.quote: The firstof these assumptions is thatrepetition priming reflects changes in the system resulting from processing of an item, changes that facilitate subsequent identification to the extentthat the sameset of processes are invoked dur ing the studyand test presentations.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Pictures prime words because task demands lead subjects to treat the drawings as linguistic objects, engaging word-structure processes even without alphabetic input.
span.quote: If the task demands encourage people to invoke processes that reflect word structure, then that is what peo ple will do, even when no alphabetic information is present.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Variability in relative priming is produced by sense (nuance) matching: priming is complete only when the same sense is accessed at study and test.
span.quote: The proposition is, in brief, that repetition priming is sense-specific, and that sense dominance is mode- and, to a lesser extent, modality-specific.

span.label: Equal relative-priming values do not entail that the same underlying processes are involved in each stimulus-class combination.
span.quote: It should be noted, of course, that the equivalence of two RP values does not logically demand the conclusion that the same processes are involved in each case.

span.label: The strategy-insensitivity result rests on a single dissociation and inherits its inferential weakness.
span.quote: This result is, of course, subject to the inferential limita tions associated with single dissociation.

span.label: The account cannot explain the observed variability in relative priming across experiments and experimenters.
span.quote: Perhaps the weakest link in our analysis involves the observed variability in RP.

span.label: The estimated picture-word priming value may hold only when pictures are treated as linguistic objects; treated as pictures, priming may vanish.
span.quote: We accept the possibility, then, that when pictures are treated as pic tures, RP will be reduced or eliminated.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: First, repetition priming of words by prior pictures is found with the PEST procedure, in which the dependent variable is accuracy of word identification (Experiments 1, 2, and 3) or the identification threshold

span.label: word identification
span.quote: Following Scarborough, Gerard, and Cortese (1979), a fifth experiment compared word identification and episodic recognition

span.label: episodic recognition
span.quote: whereas intermodal (i.e. picture-word) performance was superior in episodic recognition, a reversal which suggests that episodic recognition involves access to a distinct memory trace

span.label: memory trace
span.quote: whereas intermodal (i.e. picture-word) performance was superior in episodic recognition, a reversal which suggests that episodic recognition involves access to a distinct memory trace

span.label: **A REVERSAL BETWEEN TWO TASKS ON THE SAME MATERIAL, WHICH IS WHY DIFFICULTY CANNOT EXPLAIN IT:** `Intramodal performance was superior in word identification, WHEREAS INTERMODAL (i.e. picture-word) performance was SUPERIOR IN EPISODIC RECOGNITION, A REVERSAL which suggests that episodic recognition involves access to a DISTINCT MEMORY TRACE.` Word-word beats picture-word when the task is identification; picture-word beats word-word when the task is recognition. **The sign flips, so no account in which one condition is simply weaker can survive** - the same structural move as Finkbeiner2011's colour-versus-identity and Schmidt2010's brightness-versus-contrast, and the strongest form of dissociation evidence in this corpus
span.quote: whereas intermodal (i.e. picture-word) performance was superior in episodic recognition, a reversal which suggests that episodic recognition involves access to a distinct memory trace

span.label: **AND IT CONTRADICTS THE PROPOSITION IT SET OUT TO TEST.** Durso and Johnson (1979) held that although a printed word facilitates identification of a corresponding picture, a picture does NOT facilitate later word recognition. This paper finds that it does: `repetition priming of words by prior pictures IS FOUND with the PEST procedure, in which the dependent variable is accuracy of word identification.` **An asymmetry claimed in the literature turns out to be an artefact of the measure** - the authors say they used identification rather than naming latency `in order to avoid the range limitations in adult reading data`, and the effect appears
span.quote: First, repetition priming of words by prior pictures is found with the PEST procedure, in which the dependent variable is accuracy of word identification (Experiments 1, 2, and 3) or the identification threshold

span.label: **THE FIFTH EXPERIMENT EXISTS ONLY TO CROSS THE TWO TASKS, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN:** `Following Scarborough, Gerard, and Cortese (1979), A FIFTH EXPERIMENT COMPARED WORD IDENTIFICATION AND EPISODIC RECOGNITION.` Four experiments establish the effect in one task; the fifth puts both tasks on the same footing so their ordering can be compared. **A crossover is only available to a design that runs both tasks** - and the earlier literature, which ran them separately, could not have found it however many subjects it used
span.quote: Following Scarborough, Gerard, and Cortese (1979), a fifth experiment compared word identification and episodic recognition

span.label: contradicts → Durso & Johnson (1979) and Morton (1984) accounts of asymmetric picture-word transfer
span.quote: This outcome is inconsistent with several accounts of the relationship between word and picture identification processes (e. g., Durso & Johnson, 1979; Morton, 1984).

span.label: replicates → Scarborough, Gerard and Cortese (1979, Experiment 3) episodic recognition experiment
span.quote: Given the dis crepancy between the results of the repetition priming ex periments reported here and those reported by Scar borough et al. (1979, Experiments 1 and 2), we designed the fifth experiment as a replication of their episodic ex periment.

span.label: word identification —contrasted-with→ episodic recognition
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THE CONTRAST IS THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE SUBJECT.** These two tasks are crossed so that the ORDERING of intramodal against intermodal priming can be compared between them, and the reversal is what the fifth experiment was built to detect. Weight 0.95: the comparison is explicit and it is the paper's design. The reversal itself is quoted whole in the first sense, because it names `intramodal` and `intermodal` - which are not nodes here, since the staged text breaks `inter modal` in most of its occurrences.
span.quote: Following Scarborough, Gerard, and Cortese (1979), a fifth experiment compared word identification and episodic recognition

span.label: episodic recognition —operationalised-as→ memory trace
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — **`SUGGESTS` IS THE HEDGE AND IT IS IN THE SENTENCE THE QUOTE IS CUT FROM.** The distinct trace is an INFERENCE from the crossover, not a measurement - nothing in these experiments observes a trace. Weight 0.85 for that gap. What makes the inference strong rather than decorative is the shape of the evidence: a reversal cannot be produced by one trace read with more or less sensitivity, so a second representation is the cheapest account. The corpus should hold the inference and its distance from the data.
span.quote: whereas intermodal (i.e. picture-word) performance was superior in episodic recognition, a reversal which suggests that episodic recognition involves access to a distinct memory trace

span.label: repetition priming —operationalised-as→ word identification
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE MEASURE WAS CHOSEN TO AVOID A KNOWN CEILING AND THAT CHOICE PRODUCED THE RESULT.** The authors state they used word identification rather than naming latency `in order to avoid the range limitations in adult reading data` - and the effect Durso and Johnson could not find appears. Weight 0.9: the operationalisation is explicit, and the quote names both the procedure (PEST) and the two dependent variables (accuracy, threshold). **An operationalisation that changes the answer is worth an edge of its own**, because the disagreement in the literature is about the measure and not about the phenomenon.
span.quote: First, repetition priming of words by prior pictures is found with the PEST procedure, in which the dependent variable is accuracy of word identification (Experiments 1, 2, and 3) or the identification threshold

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A one-way analysis of variance showed that the main effectof repetition status wassignificant [F(2,46) = 18.6, P < .01].

span.label: post hoc multiple comparison test
span.quote: Comparisons conducted according to Newman Keuls showed thatthe differences between the word-word and new word conditions and between the picture-word and newword conditions weresignificant at alpha = .01.

span.label: ANOVA interaction test
span.quote: An analysis of variance conducted on the results of Ex periment 3 demonstrated that the main effect of repeti tion status [F(l, 15) = 37.4, p < .01] and the interaction between word frequency and repetition status [F(l, 15) = 8.0, p < .05] were both significant.

span.label: repeated measures ANOVA
span.quote: An analysis of variance conducted on the accuracy data from the two old conditions indicated that the main ef fect of repetition status [F(1, 17) = 278, p < .01] and the main effect of word frequency [F(1, 17) = 14.7, P < .01] were both significant

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: the studies yielded a mean picture-word value of .35 (SD = 0.22, N = 9)

span.label: meta-analysis
span.quote: but the magnitude of the variability between experiments and between experimenters is evident in the meta-analyses summarized in the introduction.

span.label: Prior exposure to a line drawing does facilitate later identification of the corresponding printed word, contradicting the claim that picture-to-word repetition transfer is absent.
span.quote: The most important result from the series of experi ments reported here is that repetition priming is observed when a test word is preceded by a line drawing of the same concept.

span.label: Intermodal (picture-word) priming is real but smaller in magnitude than intramodal (word-word) priming.
span.quote: Second, the magnitude of repetition priming under intermodal con ditions is less than that observed under intramodal condi tions, an outcome which is consistent with the modality data (Experiments 1 and 4).

span.label: The size of picture-to-word priming is unaffected by whether subjects encoded the pictures by naming or by referential size judgment, i.e. it is insensitive to study-phase strategy.
span.quote: Third, the magnitude of prim ing under intermodal conditions does not vary according to whether subjects study the initial pictures with size judg ment or naming (Experiment 2).

span.label: Word frequency modulates only the intermodal component of priming; the extra facilitation attributable to intramodal repetition is frequency-independent.
span.quote: Fourth, when repe tition effects for low-frequency and high-frequency words are compared, when the prime is either a picture or a word, there is a frequency difference for intermodal prim ing, but the additional priming attributable to intramodal effects does not vary with frequency (Experiments 3 and 4).

span.label: In episodic recognition the ordering of conditions reverses, with picture-word better than word-word, the opposite of the perceptual identification result.
span.quote: Fifth, when episodic recognition is tested, the rela tionship between the intra- and intermodal conditions is reversed, and the picture-word treatment is superior in regard to speed and accuracy (Experiment 5).

span.label: relative priming (RP)
span.quote: RP = (alternative form-control) / (same form-control),

span.label: primary processing
span.quote: By primary processing, we mean those processes that are that are necessary to establish the identity of a stimulus.

span.label: secondary processing
span.quote: Secondary processing, in contrast, involves processes that operate subsequent to, or apart from, stimulus identification.

span.label: remote repetition conditions
span.quote: The published evidence concerning transfer from pic tures to printed words under remote repetition conditions (i.e., the same item is repeated after presentation of at least seven other items) is summarized in Table 1.

span.label: mode / modality / stimulus class
span.quote: we will use the termpictures to refer to line drawings as well as photographic pictures of ob jects; mode to refer to the contrastbetween pictures and words (whether spoken or printed); modality to refer to the contrast between spoken andprinted words

span.label: repetition status (new word / picture-word / word-word)
span.quote: The design involved a single factor, repetition status, with repeated measures on each of three treatments.

span.label: word frequency (high vs low)
span.quote: The design for Experiments 3 and 4 involved two fac tors, repetition status and word frequency, with repeated measures on each factor.

span.label: study-phase encoding strategy (naming vs referential size judgment)
span.term: study-phase encoding strategy (naming vs referential size judgment)
span.quote: Third, the study phase involved either naming (Group 1) or referential size judgment (Group 2).

span.label: word identification accuracy / identification threshold
span.quote: First, repetition priming of words by prior pictures is found with the PEST procedure, in which the dependent variable is accuracy of word identification (Experiments 1, 2, and 3) or the identification threshold (Experiments 3 and 4).

span.label: PEST-derived SOA equating task difficulty across subjects
span.term: PEST-derived SOA equating task difficulty across subjects
span.quote: a derivative of PEST (parameter Estimation by SequentialTesting: Pent land, 1980) was used to ensure that subjects were tested at approximately the same level of difficulty

span.label: counterbalancing of item subsets across priming treatments
span.term: counterbalancing of item subsets across priming treatments
span.quote: The subsets were then counterbalanced across subjects so that each one appeared equally often under each of the three priming treat ments.

span.label: 0.57 — relative priming value for picture-to-word transfer obtained in Experiment 1
span.quote: The RP value for these data is 0.57.

span.label: .35 (SD = 0.22, N = 9) — mean relative priming for picture-word transfer averaged over the nine previously published studies the authors compiled
span.quote: the studies yielded a mean picture-word value of .35 (SD = 0.22, N = 9)

span.label: 55.3 % and 61.6 % vs 46.8% — word identification accuracy in the picture-word and word-word conditions compared with the new word baseline in Experiment 1
span.quote: The cor responding values for the picture-word and word-word conditions were 55.3 %and 61.6 %correct, respectively, suggesting that intermodal as well as intramodal facilita tion was present.

span.label: 14 msec (range 7 to 33) — mean PEST-derived stimulus onset asynchrony threshold for the 24 retained subjects in Experiment 1
span.quote: The mean SOA for the 24 subjects included in the final analysis was 14 msec, with individual values ranging from 7 to 33 msec.

span.label: 15.4 msec (SD = 3.2) and 12.9 msec (SD = 4.3) — 50% identification thresholds for low- and high-frequency words that had previously been seen as line drawings (Experiment 4)
span.quote: the equivalent values for Experiment 4 (words previously seen as line draw ings) were 15.4 msec (SD = 3.2) and 12.9 msec (SD = 4.3).

span.label: 48.1 % and 0.30 sec — accuracy and reaction time advantage of the picture-word over the word-word condition in the episodic recognition test
span.quote: Averaged over high- and low-frequency concepts, the mean accuracy and reaction time advantages for the picture-word condition were 48.1 % and 0.30 sec, respectively.
